input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-536: Information Retrieval. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research topics, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites: CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-536 and CSCI-636. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[postgresql-documentation]
Data systems organize records with declared types, tables, rows, columns, keys, and constraints. Queries select, join, aggregate, order, and transform data. Indexes provide additional access paths for selected workloads. Transactions group operations and isolation controls how concurrent operations observe one another. Query planning and physical storage affect performance without changing logical query meaning. Analytical work should preserve provenance from captured data through cleaning, transformation, grouping, modeling, visualization, and reporting. Data quality analysis makes missingness, duplicates, inconsistent representation, integrity constraints, sampling, and update behavior explicit.

[rit-csci-536]
An introduction to the theories and techniques used to construct search engines. Topics include search interfaces, traditional retrieval models (e.g., TF-IDF, BM25), modern retrieval techniques (e.g., neural reranking and retrieval), search engine evaluation, and search applications (e.g., conversational IR, enterprise search). Students will also review current IR research topics, and complete a group project in which they will design and execute experiments for search engine components. Prerequisites: CSCI-331 or equivalent course. Students may not take and receive credit for CSCI-536 and CSCI-636. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Spring

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Data-analysis workflows separate data preparation, exploratory analysis, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn mappings from examples paired with target labels, while unsupervised methods identify structure without targets. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine transformations and estimators so the same operations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined splits. Grouping, dimensionality reduction, classification, regression, and clustering answer different questions and require appropriate assumptions and metrics. Evaluation must match the task and the cost of errors, while distribution shift, missing data, overfitting, and unexamined sampling choices can invalidate conclusions.

beats.claim: Search engines organize digital documents into structured indexes to enable fast, relevant query responses.
beats.example: A web crawler indexes HTML pages by extracting text, building an inverted index, and storing term frequencies.
beats.title: Search Engine Architecture Overview
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing query input, index lookup, and result output with labeled components.

beats.claim: User queries are parsed and transformed into structured representations before index traversal.
beats.example: A natural language query like 'climate change effects' is tokenized and normalized to match indexed terms.
beats.title: Query Processing and Parsing
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of raw query text versus parsed query components with highlighted tokens.

beats.claim: Inverted indexes map terms to document IDs, enabling efficient retrieval of relevant documents.
beats.example: The term 'machine' points to document IDs [101, 105, 112], allowing direct access to containing pages.
beats.title: Inverted Index Construction
beats.visualDirection: Render a simplified inverted index table with term columns and document ID lists.

beats.claim: TF-IDF calculates document relevance by weighting term frequency against inverse document frequency.
beats.example: A term appearing in many documents receives a lower IDF weight, reducing its relevance score.
beats.title: TF-IDF Relevance Scoring
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate TF-IDF calculation with a small document corpus showing term frequencies and IDF values.

beats.claim: BM25 refines TF-IDF by incorporating document length normalization and position weighting.
beats.example: Short documents receive higher scores for rare terms, while BM25 adjusts scores based on term position in text.
beats.title: BM25 Ranking Algorithm
beats.visualDirection: Display a comparison table of TF-IDF versus BM25 scores for the same query across different documents.

beats.claim: Neural reranking models re-evaluate top-ranked results using deep learning representations.
beats.example: A transformer-based model scores query-document pairs by analyzing semantic similarity in high-dimensional space.
beats.title: Neural Reranking Techniques
beats.visualDirection: Show a neural network diagram with query and document embeddings merging into a relevance score output.

beats.claim: Search performance is measured using precision, recall, and NDCG to quantify relevance quality.
beats.example: Precision measures the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant, while NDCG accounts for ranking order.
beats.title: Search Evaluation Metrics
beats.visualDirection: Present a precision-recall curve and NDCG graph with labeled axes and example points.

beats.claim: Modern search systems support multi-turn dialogue and domain-specific enterprise queries.
beats.example: Enterprise search indexes internal documents with role-based access and contextual filters for business users.
beats.title: Conversational and Enterprise Search
beats.visualDirection: Show a dialogue flow for conversational search and a dashboard for enterprise search filters.

beats.claim: Search engine components are evaluated through controlled experiments comparing retrieval and ranking methods.
beats.example: A group project tests BM25 versus neural reranking on a benchmark corpus to measure score improvements.
beats.title: Experimental Design in IR
beats.visualDirection: Display an experimental setup diagram with baseline, variant, and evaluation metrics.

beats.claim: A structured checklist ensures systematic evaluation of search system performance and relevance.
beats.example: The checklist verifies index coverage, ranking consistency, metric alignment, and error cost assessment.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Show a printable checklist template with checkboxes for each evaluation criterion.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of a search engine architecture, including indexing, retrieval, and ranking.
Explain how traditional statistical models like TF-IDF and BM25 compute document relevance scores.
Apply a practical analysis checklist to evaluate search system performance using precision, recall, and NDCG.
